This Claude Basics episode walks through what the matter-update skill actually is and where its reliability ends. A skill isn't accumulated habit — it's a folder Claude reads before it acts, holding one plain-language instruction: append a dated event to the matter's history file, refresh the log row to match. It fires on five triggers — a new development, a status change, a risk reassessment, a deadline shift, a change in settlement authority — read in order, no branching unless a step says so. Open a brand-new conversation about a matter Claude has never touched, and the same steps run immediately. There's nothing to remember between conversations, because there's nothing being remembered at all.

The takeaway: ask for exactly what the file describes — a dated event, a refreshed row — and it runs the same way every time, on any matter. Ask for something the file never mentions — a strategy call, a new field, a judgment about risk — and there's nothing to guess from. It only does what's written. This is for legal teams evaluating AI case-logging tools, anyone building or auditing Claude Skills, and anyone who wants to know the difference between consistent behavior and memory before they trust either one.

Try it yourself: before Claude makes any change, ask it to read the instructions for the task in full and explain, step by step, exactly what it's about to do — which file changes, and what it won't touch unless you say so. Only then let it proceed.

title: Does Claude Already Know Every Matter You Have? (No — Here's Why)
description:
Does Claude's matter-workspace skill mean it already knows every matter you have, blended into one pool? No — by default, it stays inside the matter it's pointed at.

This Claude Basics episode walks through what a "skill" actually is and what matter-workspace specifically does with it. A skill isn't hidden logic — it's a folder holding one file, SKILL.md, plain-language instructions Claude reads before it works and follows step by step, in order, with no branching unless a step says to branch. Open a brand-new matter and ask Claude about specifics from a different case, and it can't see them. That's not a workaround — it's the design: matter-workspace walls off every matter from every other one unless cross-matter context is explicitly switched on in the practice's CLAUDE.md.

The takeaway: neither direction proves the switch's state. Watching Claude stay inside one matter doesn't prove cross-matter context is off — it might already be on. Claude missing a detail from another matter doesn't prove isolation is working — it might simply not have been asked. The only way to know is to check the skill file and the switch directly. title: Claude Wrote My Legal Memo. One Citation Was Quietly Dead
description:
Is Claude's legal memo a legal opinion? Wrong question — a memo is a working draft, not a verified answer.

This Claude Basics episode walks through what a legal memo handoff with Claude actually does, and what it doesn't. A memo that reads confidently — real cases named correctly, holdings stated plainly — can still be wrong in a way that's invisible on the page. The video walks through a real gap: a citation that names the right case and the right holding, except that case was overruled last year. It reads exactly like every citation around it that's still good law. That's the case for a memo built on three parts: the legal question and facts going in, a structured issue-rule-application-conclusion analysis coming out, and a required verification step before anyone relies on it.

The takeaway: an unflagged citation isn't automatically confirmed — no flag means no one has looked yet, not that it's clean. And a memo that comes back heavily corrected at the verification step isn't a failure; that's the check doing exactly what it's supposed to do. A memo is reliable once every citation in it has been checked against the law as it stands today, not because it reads confidently. This is for anyone using AI to draft first-pass legal analysis, law students and associates learning how AI fits into memo workflows, and anyone curious about where AI drafting is genuinely useful — and where human verification stays non-negotiable.

Try it yourself: take a real legal question, ask Claude to draft an issue-rule-application-conclusion memo with every case citation flagged to check, then verify each citation against current law before anyone treats the memo as reliable.

title: Claude Reviewed My NDA. Here's Why "Nothing Flagged" Isn't a Green Light
description:
Can Claude clear your NDA? Wrong question — here's the right one.

This Claude Basics episode walks through what an NDA review with Claude actually does, and what it doesn't. A clean pass — no flags — feels like a green light. It isn't. The video walks through a real gap: a confidentiality clause missing the standard carve-out for information that later becomes public, sitting right next to clauses that have it. It reads complete. It isn't. That's the case for a review built on three parts: the clauses going in, a check against a baseline of standard terms (definitions, carve-outs, duration, mutuality), and a flag list of what's unusual coming out.

The takeaway: flagged means check this, not reject this — and a clause with no flag isn't the same as a clause a lawyer signed off on. Only a check against the law that actually applies (carve-out and duration norms vary by state and by deal) moves a clause from flagged to either fine or something that needs to change. This is for anyone using AI tools to do a first pass on contracts, freelancers and founders reviewing NDAs before signing, and anyone curious about where AI-assisted legal review is genuinely useful — and where it stops.

Try it yourself: paste an NDA into Claude, ask it to check against standard confidentiality carve-outs (public information, independent development, prior knowledge, legally required disclosure), flag anything missing or unusual, then have someone who knows the applicable law check every flagged clause before you sign.

title: Only the Terminal Says Yes. — The Discord Access-Control Skill
description:
Claude's Discord access skill keeps its whole state in one file,
access.json, with five fields: the DM policy, an allow list, per-channel
groups, pending pairing codes, and the patterns that trigger the bot. If
the file is missing, Claude just uses safe defaults. But before any of
those fields get touched, one rule runs first: if the request arrived as
a message on Discord rather than something you typed yourself, Claude
refuses it. Approving someone follows one path — pair, with a code —
that checks the code hasn't expired, adds the person to the allow list,
and writes a marker file the Discord side watches for. Two rules guard
it: always read the file fresh before writing, and never auto-pick a
pending code, even if there's only one. Here's why that last rule
matters: someone could DM the bot to seed a pending code, then send a
second message posing as you — approve the pending request. Refusing
anything that isn't typed in your own terminal is exactly what stops
that second message from working.

title: Your Agent Never Fires If Its Description Lists Skills
description:
An agent's description is what decides whether Claude dispatches it at all. Describe when to use it — not what it does.

An agent file is two things: YAML frontmatter, then a markdown system-prompt body.

THE FIVE FRONTMATTER FIELDS

name — lowercase with hyphens, 3 to 50 characters, starting and ending alphanumeric. code-reviewer, test-generator, security-analyzer.

description — the field that matters most, because it's loaded into context whenever the agent is registered. It's what decides whether Claude dispatches this agent at all.

model — inherit is the recommended default.

color — visual distinction in the interface, nothing more.

tools — the array of permissions the agent actually gets. Give it only what the task needs.

TWO LOCATIONS, ONE JOB EACH

The description has one job: state exactly when Claude should reach for this agent, not just what it can do. The format is "Use this agent when...", then "Typical triggers include" with two to four concrete scenarios, then a pointer to a When to invoke section in the body. That prose names real triggers — proactive and reactive, different phrasings of the same request — and says when not to use the agent.

The body's own When to invoke section repeats this in more depth: a bold scenario name, what the situation looks like, what the agent should actually do.

Two different jobs. The description is for Claude's dispatch decision. The body is for the agent once it's already running.

THE CATCH

Nothing keeps the two in sync. If the trigger scenarios change and only the description gets updated, the body's When to invoke section goes stale — or the other way around. And it's the description alone that Claude reads to decide whether to dispatch at all, so a scenario that only lives in the stale body section never even gets checked at that moment.

Keeping both current by hand, every time triggers change, is the actual maintenance cost of this design.

YOUR TURN

Paste this into Claude:

Create an agent for my plugin that reviews pull request diffs for security issues.

Then check the description Claude wrote. Does it say "Use this agent when..." with two to four concrete trigger scenarios, or does it just list what the agent does? Does the body have a When to invoke section with worked scenarios? Are the tools it picked the minimum needed — probably Read and Bash, not Write?

Run that today, on your own plugin idea — not the video's example.

title: MCP Apps: Your Tool Doesn't Serve the Widget's HTML
description:
Does your tool serve the widget's HTML? No — a separate resource does. Here's the two-part registration pattern.

An MCP app is a standard MCP server that also serves interactive UI, rendered inline in the chat surface as an iframe.

THE TWO-PART REGISTRATION

Part one, the tool. It declares a UI resource, and its handler returns plain data — not the HTML.

Part two, the resource, registered separately. It serves the widget's HTML with the exact MIME type constant.

The host sees the resource URI, fetches the resource, renders it in an iframe, and pipes the tool's return value in through an event. Inside the iframe, an App class bridges the two sides — sendMessage, updateModelContext, callServerTool, openLink — set up before it connects.

One step is mandatory: the frame's content security policy blocks CDN script fetches, so the widget script bundle has to be inlined directly into the HTML at startup.

ROUTE FIRST, BUILD SECOND

Elicitation is spec-native. Zero UI code, works in any compliant host. Use it for yes/no confirmation, short enums, and flat forms.

Build a widget only when elicitation can't meet the need: large or searchable lists that need scrolling, visual previews before choosing, charts and maps, live-updating progress.

If none of those apply, skip the widget entirely. Text is faster to build and faster for the user.

FIVE RULES THAT SAVE REWRITES

One widget per tool. The tool's description must mention the widget — that's what makes Claude reach for it. Graceful degradation is automatic; hosts without the app surface just render the tool's text content. Don't block on widget results for display-only tools. Return a text summary alongside so Claude can keep reasoning. And follow the host's theme once connected instead of hard-coding one.

TWO CAUSES, ONE BLANK RECTANGLE

Serve the widget with the wrong MIME type and the host silently refuses to render it. Leave the ext-apps bundle un-inlined and the content security policy blocks the CDN fetch — the widget stays blank there too.

Same failure, two different causes, and the browser console won't tell you which one it was. Get the type or the bundle wrong and it fails blank, not loud.

YOUR TURN

Paste this into Claude:

Build an MCP app with a file-picker widget that lets someone choose a file from a list a directory-scan tool returns.

Then check four things. Does it use two-part registration — a tool with _meta.ui.resourceUri plus a separate resource? Does the resource use the exact MIME type constant, not a hand-typed string? Is the ext-apps bundle inlined at startup instead of pulled from a CDN? And does the tool still return real text content alongside the widget, so a host without the app surface still sees something useful?

Run that today, on your own MCP server — not the video's example.

title: Build an MCP Server: Four Questions Before Any Code
description:
Ask Claude to build an MCP server and it doesn't write code — it asks four questions first. Here's why the order matters.

Deployment. Users. How many actions. Auth. Get that order backwards and you're not tweaking the server later, you're rewriting it.

THREE DEPLOYMENT PATHS, RANKED

Remote HTTP wins by default for anything wrapping a cloud API. Zero install friction, one server serves all users, and OAuth flows work properly with redirect handling. Recommend it unless the server must touch the user's local machine.

MCPB — Model Context Protocol Bundle — packages a server with its runtime for local distribution. The sanctioned way to ship when the server reads local files, drives a desktop app, or talks to localhost services.

Local stdio via npx is fine for personal prototypes but painful to distribute. A stepping stone, with the MCPB upgrade path flagged from the start.

TWO TOOL-DESIGN PATTERNS

Pattern A — one tool per action. Under about fifteen operations, give each a dedicated tool with a tight description and schema. Claude reads the list once and knows exactly what's possible.

Pattern B — search plus execute. Wrapping a large API with dozens to hundreds of endpoints, listing every operation floods the context window and degrades model performance. Expose two tools instead: search_actions returns matching operations for a natural-language intent, execute_action runs one by ID. Context stays lean.

The hybrid promotes the three to five most-used actions to dedicated tools and keeps the long tail behind search and execute.

Beyond tools, the other three primitives are resources (host-browsable docs and data), prompts (user-triggered commands), and elicitation (spec-native mid-tool user input, without building UI). Most servers only need tools — knowing the others prevents reinventing wheels.

THE DESCRIPTION DECIDES

Once the server exists, Claude picks a tool by reading its description, not its name. A description that just restates the name — "creates an issue" for create_issue — doesn't tell Claude when to reach for it over a similar tool like update_issue. The more specific the description, the more reliably Claude calls the right one at the right moment.

YOUR TURN

Paste this into Claude:

Build an MCP server that wraps the GitHub API — tools for creating issues, searching repositories, and getting pull request details.

Then watch four things. Does it ask discovery questions before writing any code, or start scaffolding right away? Does it recommend remote HTTP as the default, and say why? Does it use one tool per action, since three tools is well under the search-plus-execute threshold? And are the tool descriptions specific enough to tell create_issue apart from update_issue?

A description that just repeats the tool's name is the tell that it skipped the tool-design guidance. Run that today, on your own API idea — not the video's example.

title: Bundling an MCP Server as an MCPB Doesn't Make It Safe
description:
Bundling your MCP server as an MCPB makes it runnable without a dev toolchain. It doesn't make it safe. Here's the difference.

It's easy to assume the bundle itself got safer along with the packaging — like putting the code in a container. Open the manifest and there's no permissions block, no sandbox field, nothing to check. A packaged MCPB runs with exactly the same file access as the original, unpackaged script. Package a path bug into it and it walks outside its own folder exactly as easily.

WHAT AN MCPB ACTUALLY IS

A zip. A manifest.json, a server folder with your code and dependencies, and an icon. The host reads the manifest and launches mcp_config's command exactly as written — ${__dirname} for bundle-relative paths, ${user_config.*} for install-time values like a folder the user picked.

THE ANCHOR: ONE ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE

Say your manifest launches the server with one setting — an environment variable named ROOT_DIR, pointing at the folder the user chose at install time. That single variable carries two real traps.

TRAP ONE — THE NAME HAS TO MATCH EXACTLY

The env var name is exactly what you wrote in the manifest. No auto-prefix, no transform. Write ROOT_DIR in the manifest but read ROOT_DIRECTORY in your server code and the value comes back silently empty. No error. No crash. The config is just quietly ignored.

TRAP TWO — A CORRECT NAME STILL ISN'T A CHECK

Get the name right and that path flows straight into your handler with no validation on it at all, because there's no sandbox to add one for you. One unvalidated ../ in a filename walks the server right out of its own folder.

NEITHER RESULT IS PROOF

An MCPB that runs fine on your machine doesn't prove it's safe anywhere else — it may only prove your own dev toolchain quietly filled a gap. And an MCPB that fails on a clean machine doesn't mean the packaging step is broken; it usually means one dependency never got bundled in.

Packaging makes a server runnable without a toolchain. The env var name still has to match exactly, and every path check is still yours to write.

YOUR TURN

Paste this into Claude:

Build an MCPB that reads files from a directory I configure at install time. Watch three things: does the env var name in the manifest's mcp_config exactly match what the server code reads? Does the server validate that every requested path stays inside that configured root, or would a ../ escape it? And does the build script bundle dependencies with esbuild, or does it assume node_modules will already be there?

It forces you to check both traps against a build you actually watch happen.

title: I Changed One File on My Cardputer. Do I Reinstall It All?
description:
Changed one file on your Cardputer? You don't reinstall everything — there's a script for exactly that. Here's which one.

The Cardputer runs MicroPython on a /flash/ filesystem. main.py is the launcher: it scans /flash/apps/ at boot and lists every .py file it finds as a menu entry, automatically. Drop a new file into that folder, push it to the device, and it shows up on the next boot. No registration code anywhere.

THE PAYLOAD, IN THREE ZONES

The launcher itself. A shared library — BLE, UI, state, protocol. And the apps folder holding whatever's installed. When you write a new app you start from hello_cardputer.py, the smallest working example: keyboard polling, font rendering, and the convention for exiting back to the launcher.

FOUR SCRIPTS, ONE JOB EACH

install_apps.py pushes the entire apps folder over USB-serial. Reach for it when you've added or renamed files and need the whole directory back in sync.
push.py pushes just the files you name. Reach for it when you've edited one existing file and want the fast loop.
tail_serial.py streams the device's serial logs. Run it in a second terminal while you test.
repl_run.py runs a single Python expression over the REPL. Handy for a quick filesystem check without pushing anything.

All four need PORT — whatever the provisioning step detected earlier.

THE OVERLAP THAT BITES

install_apps.py and push.py can both push your one changed file. install_apps.py syncs the complete apps folder every time, which takes longer than it needs to for a single edit. push.py, given just that one filename, does the same job in a fraction of the time.

Nothing in either script's name tells you which is faster for the change in front of you. That's a distinction you have to remember. The tools don't remind you of it. Match the script to the size of the change, not to habit.

YOUR TURN

Paste this into Claude:

Add a timer app to the Cardputer that counts down from 60 seconds and returns to the launcher when done.

Then watch four things. Does it create the new file in buddy/device/apps/, following the hello_cardputer.py structure? Does it use push.py for the single new file rather than install_apps.py for the full directory? Does it follow the exit convention — polling the keyboard for a key back to the launcher — instead of hard-looping with no way out? And after pushing, does it suggest tail_serial.py to watch the output, instead of asking you to re-flash?

Run that today, on your own Cardputer. Not just in your head.

title: Can Claude Build My Claude Code Automations? Not Quite
description:
Can Claude build your Claude Code automations? No. It recommends them — and here's exactly where the recommendation stops.

The Automation Recommender is a read-only analysis skill. It scans your codebase for signals — language and framework, existing Claude config, test setup, CI files, database and API code — then recommends automations across all five Claude Code extensibility types.

THE FIVE TYPES

Hooks run automatically on tool events: format on save, block a risky edit, run tests after a change.
Subagents are specialized agents Claude runs in parallel: a code reviewer, a security auditor, a test writer.
Skills are packaged workflows, invoked deliberately by Claude or a slash command.
Plugins bundle related skills for one-step install.
MCP servers reach outside Claude entirely — databases, APIs, browsers, documentation.

Same question for all five: what triggers it, and how wide is its scope?

HOW THE SKILL WORKS

It reads your codebase, matches what it finds to a specific recommendation one type at a time, then caps it — one or two per category, the most valuable pick rather than an exhaustive dump — and tells you that you can ask for more. Then it writes a report: your codebase profile, one section per automation type, each with what to add and why it fits.

THE CATCH

Recommending isn't the same as handing you a runnable step. For a subagent, it points at a template file instead of writing the scaffold inline. For a plugin, it names the plugin but not the install command. It's read-only end to end. It never edits your files — and it never finishes that last step either. The distance between "here's what to add" and "here's the exact command" is yours to close.

Then check two things the recommender doesn't always give you: for any subagent it suggests, does it write the actual agent file, or just point you at a template? title: Claude, Gl Recon.
description:
Claude picked up a skill called gl-recon — does that mean it's now deciding which ledger is right and fixing the books? No. It matches the general ledger to the subledger at the trade date, position, or transaction level, surfaces every place they disagree, and tags each disagreement with a likely cause. Run it on a period with a known break and neither ledger number moves — only a classified break sits between them. Say the GL shows $104,000 for a position and the subledger shows $100,000: gl-recon flags the $4,000 gap and tags it, say, a late trade. That makes it a matcher and a classifier, not a fixer — the payoff is the same breaks caught the same way, every run; the limit is that it never decides which ledger is correct. And neither a tidy classification nor a clean reconciliation is proof on its own: a break tagged "timing" doesn't prove it resolves itself, and a period that reconciles clean doesn't prove nothing was wrong in it.

title: Claude, Idea Generation.
description:
Claude picked up a skill called idea-generation — does that mean it's now creatively brainstorming new stock ideas, the way an analyst free-associates in a pitch meeting? No. It runs a systematic screen: quantitative screens, thematic research, and pattern recognition, in that fixed order, to surface long and short candidates. Run the same screen twice on the same data and you get the same candidates back both times — not two different creative pitches. Say the criteria are rising free cash flow plus recent insider buying: idea-generation runs the screen, checks the thematic angle, looks for the pattern, and three candidates surface. Run it again tomorrow with the same criteria, and the same three candidates surface — not a fresh set, not a new pitch. That makes it a screener, not a strategist — the payoff is the same criteria surfacing the same candidates, every run; the limit is that it only finds what fits the screen you wrote. And neither result is proof on its own: a candidate surfacing doesn't prove it's a good trade, and a stock that never surfaces isn't proven bad.

title: Claude, Nav Tieout.
description:
Claude picked up a skill called nav-tieout — does that mean it's now verifying
that the fund's NAV is correct? No. It assumes the NAV pack is right, and ties
an LP statement to it: recompute the LP's capital account from the NAV
components, then flag any line that doesn't agree. Run it on a period with a
known LP-statement error and the fund's NAV components are exactly what they
were before the run — only a flagged mismatch shows up on the LP side. Say
the NAV pack puts the account at $404,000 and the LP statement shows
$400,000: nav-tieout flags the $4,000 gap and leaves it there. That makes it
a checker, not an auditor of the fund — the payoff is the same mismatch
caught the same way, every time, before the statement goes out; the limit is
that it never questions whether the NAV pack itself is right. And neither
result is proof on its own: a flagged mismatch doesn't prove the LP statement
is wrong (the NAV pack could be the one with the error), and a clean tie-out
doesn't prove the NAV was calculated correctly — it only means the two
documents agree with each other.

**Topic:** CLAUDE · SKILLS

description:
The instinct the day an M&A deal closes is to write an integration plan — a
single document laying out what has to happen. But a plan captures one

title: Should You Respond to an Infringement Letter Right Away?
description:
A newcomer's first instinct on an infringement or cease-and-desist letter is
to respond right away — the language reads like a fire (cease-and-desist,
a threat to sue, a deadline in bold). But most incoming claims are form
letters mailed to hundreds of companies at once, with no evidence attached
and nothing specific to your product. Rushing every one of those to counsel
just delays the one that's actually different. What decides urgency is four
checks: who's asserting the claim, what specific right they're claiming,
what evidence is attached, and what deadline is demanded. Watch the anchor:
a letter claiming your packaging copies a competitor's — all exclamation
points, no attachments — until it's run through those four checks, you
can't tell whether it's noise or the one that matters. Clearing every check
doesn't prove a claim is valid, and a bare form letter isn't zero risk
forever either.

title: When Should You Update the Handbook?
description:
An employee handbook usually gets written once and reviewed on a schedule —
maybe once a year. That feels responsible, but it misses the actual
trigger: a law that changes in March doesn't wait for the December
read-through. The section it touches is wrong the day the law takes
effect, and it stays wrong for however many months are left until the
scheduled review. Watch the anchor: a state raises its paid-leave minimum
in the spring — that one change touches exactly one section, the leave
policy, and gets logged with what changed, why, and when it took effect.
Being flagged doesn't mean the new language is finished — it still needs a
legal read — and a quiet quarter doesn't mean the handbook is complete,
only that no tracked law changed.

title: What Comes First When You Hire Abroad?
description:
Hiring your first person in a new country? The contract is the last thing you should write, not the first.

A contract's label doesn't decide how a role is classified. The country's labor law does. Call someone a contractor while you set their hours, hand them your equipment, and stand as their only client — a local court will read that relationship as an employee's, whatever the page says.

Three checks come before any contract gets drafted:

1. How the role is classified under local labor law
2. Who the legal employer is on paper — your own entity, or an Employer of Record standing in
3. Which local rules are mandatory regardless of the contract — notice periods, statutory benefits, termination rules

Run the example through it: a developer in Berlin, forty hours a week, one client, working on that client's laptop with that client's tools. Employee-shaped, no matter what the contract calls them.

Two things that follow. Passing as contractor-shaped today doesn't lock it in — change how the work actually runs and the classification can flip under the same contract. And landing on employee-shaped doesn't mean you need your own German entity tomorrow; an Employer of Record can be the legal employer on paper while you sort that out.

YOUR TURN — paste this into Claude:

"I'm planning to hire our first employee in a new country. Before drafting anything, walk me through how the role would likely be classified there under local labor law, the difference between opening our own entity there versus using an Employer of Record, and which statutory terms — notice period, benefits, termination rules — would apply once it's classified."

It forces the classification and legal-employer questions to the front, before a single clause gets written.

title: What Is a Gap-Surfacer Actually Looking For?
description:
Does Claude catch bad contract clauses? No — a gap check only catches missing ones. Here's the difference, and why it matters.

A checklist gap check does one thing: it walks a list of items a document is supposed to contain, scans for matching text, and reports the items with no match anywhere. It is not judging whether a clause is any good. It's only asking whether something is there.

Watch the anchor beat in this one. The assignment-clause line comes back with no match — flagged. But the protection was there the whole time, filed under "Transfer of Rights" instead of "Assignment." The checklist's wording missed it.

That's the carry-out: a match doesn't prove a clause is good enough, and a no-match doesn't prove it's actually gone. Both times, a person still has to open the page and read it. A flag is a pointer to look, not a finished finding.

YOUR TURN — paste this into Claude:

"I have a document and a short checklist of things it's supposed to include. Scan the document, flag every checklist item with no matching text anywhere in it, and for each flag, tell me whether equivalent coverage might exist under different wording before calling it missing."

title: What Does a Feature-Risk-Assessment Actually Tell You?
description:
Asking Claude to run a feature-risk-assessment before a feature ships can
sound like asking for a safe/not-safe verdict. It isn't one. Take a feature
that looks harmless on a quick look — users upload a photo ID to prove
their age. The checklist asks a different question: where does that photo
go, how long is it kept, who can see it. Read the SKILL.md, work through it
step by step, and what comes back is four filled-in boxes — what's
collected, where it's stored, how long it's kept, who can access it — not
a judgment. All four boxes filled doesn't mean the feature is safe, and one
flag raised doesn't mean it gets killed. Either way, someone now has what
they need to decide.

title: Type III Error Detector — Wrong Problem, Right Solution
description:
Type III Error Detector — When Claude's Answer Is Right and the Problem Is Wrong
Description

Ask Claude to cut support-ticket volume, and one answer comes back fast: hide the contact button. The ticket count really does drop. The ask is technically satisfied — and completely wrong, because nothing about why people needed help got fixed. Statistician Howard Raiffa had a name for solving the wrong problem correctly: a Type III error. AI is particularly good at making them, because it optimizes the objective you wrote down, not the one you meant.

title: Are You Supervising Claude at the Right Level?
description:
Are You Supervising Claude at the Right Level? — Three Levels of AI Supervision, Explained
Description

Most people assume trusting AI "the right amount" means picking one comfort level — a quick glance, a nod — and keeping it steady no matter what they asked for. It doesn't work that way. Renaming a variable and asking Claude to propose a system architecture are not the same task. Sheridan and Verplank catalogued ten levels of automation back in 1978; applied to AI, three matter: Level One, copy-paste use; Level Two, research-level use; Level Three, true collaboration. Watch the anchor: Priya, on one ordinary afternoon, gives the exact same quick glance to a variable rename (fine, that's calibrated), a market-size citation (below the line), and a full architecture proposal (far below it). A simple rule flags the mismatch — short checking on high-stakes work — one flag: applying a 1978 framework to AI chat is this reel's adaptation, not Sheridan and Verplank's own claim. Run the flag on Priya's afternoon and it catches exactly what you'd expect — but a flag only proves the checking didn't match the stakes, not that the answer was wrong, and no flag doesn't prove nothing was missed. Trusting AI the right amount isn't a fixed habit. It's calibrated to what you actually handed it, task by task.

title: How Do You Know If You're Supervising Claude Enough?
description:
Ask most people if they check Claude's work carefully enough and they'll answer
with a feeling — careful, or not careful enough. That's the wrong measurement.
Supervision should scale with how much decision-making you actually hand over
on a given task, not stay flat as a personal habit. The fix: log it. A small
tool logs each interaction, classifies how much you handed to Claude — a quick
edit, an assisted task, or a real decision made mostly by the model — and once
a week, audits for the gap: high-autonomy interactions that got almost no
verification time. Watch the anchor: twelve real interactions plotted on a
grid, usage against verification time. Nine land near the diagonal. Three sit
in a danger corner — heavy reliance, almost no checking. Two weeks later the
danger corner should empty out, and that's real progress — but a rising score
only proves you logged more checking time, not that the checking caught
anything, and an un-flagged interaction just means this pass didn't catch it.
Supervision isn't one habit you either have or don't. It's a gap between trust
and verification, invisible until you log it.

title: Solve-Verify Asymmetry
description:
No Verification Path, No Delegation — the Verification Matrix, Explained
Description

Claude can hand back a citation, a claim, and a quantified number in the same paragraph, in exactly the same confident voice. Fluent, assured prose is a training habit — it looks identical whether the content underneath is verified or invented. So the natural move is to proofread: read it over, check that it flows. If it reads clean, it feels checked. It isn't: a fabricated citation, formatted exactly like a real one, passes every read-through. Only opening the actual source catches it.

Editing asks "is this clear?" Auditing asks "is this true, traceable, and supported by the source?" — two different questions, and editing never opens the source. The verification matrix assigns the right check per output type before you read for clarity: a citation means opening the source, a number means recomputing a sample and checking the denominator, a claim means tracing it to one specific sentence. The depth of that check should match the consequence — light for personal notes, moderate for an internal document, strict for anything published, submitted, or signed. A client email is strict, because the consequence is yours.

From Humanitarians AI: short, plain explanations of how Claude actually works, for a general audience meeting Claude for the first time. Liam, in for Professor Bear.

In this one: why fluent prose isn't an accuracy signal; the difference between editing and auditing; how the verification matrix assigns a check per output type; the one flag worth knowing (the matrix assumes you can reach the primary source); and both directions — what passing every check proves, and what a single failed check does not.

title: Silent Omission Signal.
description:
An agent asked to summarize a folder of files processes whatever it can
reach and presents the result as the whole picture — no error message, no
warning, no count of files skipped. The brief still reads fluent and
confident. This happens because agents optimize toward task completion: a
tool-call failure (a folder not found, a file not readable) gets logged
internally, not surfaced in the output, unless the task explicitly asked for
it — silence is the path of least resistance, not a malfunction. The
recognition sign is an absence: a complete run should carry a count ("eight
documents found, eight processed"); when that count is missing, the
omission may be silent. The fix is one added instruction — require an
inventory artifact before the summary: items in scope, items processed,
items skipped, items denied. A matching count doesn't prove the rest of the
summary is accurate, and a mismatch doesn't always mean something important
was lost — but without the count, there's no way to tell which case you're
in.

title: No Verification Path, No Delegation
description:
No Verification Path, No Delegation — the Verification Matrix, Explained
Description

Claude can hand back a citation, a claim, and a quantified number in the same paragraph, in exactly the same confident voice. Fluent, assured prose is a training habit — it looks identical whether the content underneath is verified or invented. So the natural move is to proofread: read it over, check that it flows. If it reads clean, it feels checked. It isn't: a fabricated citation, formatted exactly like a real one, passes every read-through. Only opening the actual source catches it.

Editing asks "is this clear?" Auditing asks "is this true, traceable, and supported by the source?" — two different questions, and editing never opens the source. The verification matrix assigns the right check per output type before you read for clarity: a citation means opening the source, a number means recomputing a sample and checking the denominator, a claim means tracing it to one specific sentence. The depth of that check should match the consequence — light for personal notes, moderate for an internal document, strict for anything published, submitted, or signed. A client email is strict, because the consequence is yours.

From Humanitarians AI: short, plain explanations of how Claude actually works, for a general audience meeting Claude for the first time. Liam, in for Professor Bear.

In this one: why fluent prose isn't an accuracy signal; the difference between editing and auditing; how the verification matrix assigns a check per output type; the one flag worth knowing (the matrix assumes you can reach the primary source); and both directions — what passing every check proves, and what a single failed check does not.

title: Why More Automation Creates More Supervision Work, Not Less — Bainbridge's Irony, Explained
description:
Why More Automation Creates More Supervision Work, Not Less — Bainbridge's Irony, Explained


A developer hands a bug fix to her AI agent. It reads the files, edits the code, reruns the tests, and reports back: resolved. The natural guess is that a more capable agent means less work for the person supervising it — capability up, workload down, one lever pulling the other. It's backwards. Now she has to read the diff, verify the tests, check for a missed edge case, and confirm nothing outside scope got touched — more deliberate work, not less. This is Bainbridge's Irony, named in 1983: automation doesn't eliminate human work, it relocates it upstream into design and into checkpoints at the end. Watch the anchor: a naive lever where capability rises and workload falls, then the real one where both arms rise together — and Priya, who moves twenty files by hand alone, or reorganizes two hundred with an agent by writing a scope, reviewing a taxonomy, approving batches, verifying counts, and auditing spot-checks. Fewer hours. More deliberate decisions. It holds for small, reversible tasks and flips once the agent's reach is wide, where one wrong scope statement becomes two hundred wrong moves. More capable agents don't reduce human work — they relocate it: upstream into the scope you write before delegating, and into the checkpoint you run after.

title: Material Plan Change: Stop Before the Scope Shifts
description:
Material Plan Change: Stop Before the Scope Shifts — Teaching Claude Agents When to Pause
Description

An agent that adapts mid-task isn't misbehaving — a tool failing, a file going missing, a format coming in wrong are ordinary parts of how these systems work. The natural fix is to let it keep going and read a report afterward. But by the time that report exists, the library is already installed and the shared folder is already read — changes nobody approved. Three signs mark a change worth stopping for: a different tool than the one approved, data beyond what was named, or a risk level higher than the plan described. Catch any one of them, and the question is only where the check sits: a report written after the fact is an audit log; a question asked before the step is supervision, and only supervision can still change what happens.

From Humanitarians AI: short, plain explanations of how Claude actually works, for a general audience meeting Claude for the first time. Liam, in for Professor Bear.

Claude can hand back a citation, a claim, and a number in the same fluent paragraph, in

accurate paragraph and the invented one come from the exact same process. Even the

title: An Agent That Finishes First Can Be Worse Than One That Stops
description:
An Agent That Finishes First Can Be Worse Than One That Stops — the Silent Omission Trap
Description

An agent can read ninety files, finish the job, and report "done" — in exactly the same confident tone whether it saw everything in scope or missed a third of it. So the natural read: if the agent says the task is complete, it must have gone through everything there was to go through. Here's the case that breaks it — an agent drafted a six-bullet brief with a clear recommendation, and it shipped to leadership. Two days later, someone found three dissenting documents sitting in a subfolder the agent never opened, one of which said the opposite of the recommendation. No error had ever appeared.

Here's the mechanism: an agent works through a job one operation at a time, and each step only reports on itself — it doesn't know what it couldn't reach, whether that's a folder it lacked permission for, a scanned page that wouldn't parse, or a file that scrolled past in a long listing. A crash tells you something went wrong; a silent omission doesn't. The completion report is built from successful operations, not a census of everything that existed.

Description

Five teammates each use Claude carefully, on their own account — surely that adds up to a careful team? Not when agents act on shared assets. title: Teaching an AI to Grade Its Own Homework
description:
Teaching an AI to Grade Its Own Homework — Constitutional AI's Self-Critique Loop

Description

Claude is partly trained by critiquing and revising its own harmful answers. If the same model both answers and grades, isn't that just an AI grading its own homework — and why would anyone trust the grade? Human harmlessness labeling is expensive, inconsistent, and doesn't generalize to new harms. Constitutional AI replaces most of it with a loop: elicit a problematic response, critique it against one specific written principle from a fixed list of sixteen, revise it to follow that principle, then use the revision as the training example — AI feedback instead of human feedback.

The result matched human-labeled training on harmlessness and beat it on helpfulness, because human graders reward caution and over-refuse. And the model can cite the exact rule it followed — a human grader's gut feeling can't be cited that way.

But two things this doesn't prove: matching on harmlessness doesn't mean the check is unbiased, since the same model both answers and grades — a shared blind spot isn't caught by that same model applying the rule to itself. That's flagged by researchers, not resolved. And beating on helpfulness doesn't mean the model is more correct, only that it refuses less; telling those apart takes a separate check.

title: Why One Always-Present Token Secretly Hijacks Every Attention Statistic — YouTube metadata
description:
Why One Always-Present Token Secretly Hijacks Every Attention Statistic
Description

Attention weights have to sum to one on every single row, whether or not any position actually deserves the mass. Look at one real head — layer four, head three, across fifty thousand sentences — and token zero, the sentence-start marker, wins the max-attention position in 91% of them, with more than half the weight every time. It isn't a discovery about meaning: token zero is present in every sequence and carries no sentence-specific content, so it's the cheapest place for a head to park leftover attention when nothing else is strongly preferred. Any statistic built from the max — "which position gets the most attention" — reports that sink, not the sentence structure you actually wanted to see. In a worked example, the real verb-to-subject dependency only shows up once the sink position is excluded from the count.

From Humanitarians AI: short, plain explanations of how Claude actually works, for a general audience meeting Claude for the first time. Liam, in for Professor Bear.

In this one: the natural assumption that a position winning the attention max almost every time must be carrying real meaning; the mechanism that breaks it (softmax must spend its mass somewhere, and an always-present, meaning-empty token is the low-resistance seat); a worked example with the raw numbers; and the two-sided limit of the result — a dominant sink doesn't mean a head learned nothing, and a head that avoids one sink token may just be parking on a different one.

title: Fluent Isn't Legitimate
description:
Fluent Isn't Legitimate — Auditing AI Answers with Suchman's Three Types of Legitimacy
Description

A confident, fluent AI answer feels trustworthy — but fluency is only ever an answer to one question: does it feel taken for granted, natural? Sociologist Mark Suchman's 1995 framework splits organizational legitimacy into three separate questions: does it serve the stakeholder's interest (pragmatic); is someone accountable for it (moral); does it feel right, taken for granted (cognitive). Put the identical AI answer in two rooms — a finance committee reviewing a projection, and a hospital bedside — and the same fluent sentence can hold in one and fail in the other, because the rooms differ in who is named to answer for it, not in how the sentence reads. The fix isn't asking the AI to sound more careful — it's naming an accountable party and a review step before the answer gets acted on.

From Humanitarians AI: short, plain explanations of how Claude actually works, for a general audience meeting Claude for the first time. Liam, in for Professor Bear.

In this one: the natural shortcut of treating a fluent answer as already legitimate on every count; the falsifying case — a named CFO versus no one named, same sentence, different verdict; the fix of naming an accountable party and a review step before the answer is acted on; and the two-sided limit — a fluent answer proves nothing about who's accountable, and disclosure or hedging doesn't fix the gap either.

title: "Verified" Isn't Evidence — How to Build a Real Verification Protocol with Claude
description:
\"Verified" Isn't Evidence — How to Build a Real Verification Protocol with Claude
Description

When an agent says a task is "verified," that word can mean the agent double-checked its own reasoning — not that anything independent was actually confirmed. A citation-matching check that runs on the same process that made the original error can re-confirm a wrong citation as "verified," because the check never leaves the agent's own say-so. The fix isn't more scrutiny after the fact — it's naming the evidence artifact before the task starts: the output type, the independent evidence that would confirm it worked, the specific check for the likeliest failure, and the artifact that has to exist afterward. title: Consensus Isn't Verification
description:
Consensus Isn't Verification — Why AI Judges Agreeing Doesn't Prove They're Right
Description

It's increasingly common to have one AI system check another one's work — grading an answer, reviewing code, auditing a claim. When several AI reviewers agree, that agreement gets treated as proof. It feels like getting a second medical opinion. It isn't one.

The test: give an AI judge the same two answers twice, just with the order swapped. Nothing about the answers changed — but the judge's verdict flips. It picked whichever answer came first, not whichever was better. That's positional bias, one of three documented, structural judging biases (position, length, style) that show up whenever an AI checks another AI's output.

From Humanitarians AI: short, plain explanations of how Claude actually works, for a general audience meeting Claude for the first time. Liam, in for Professor Bear.

title: The Verifier Never Sees Your Thinking
description:
Claude's math-olympiad skill checks a problem's reading before it ever
starts solving — competition problems often bury an easy reading next to
the hard one, and in past runs most errors came from solving the wrong
reading entirely. Once the intended reading is settled, eight to twelve
solvers tackle it in parallel, each iterating on its own with no
calculator and no code, reasoning only. Before any proof reaches a
verifier, everything except the finished argument is deleted — every
false start, every scratch note. Fresh verifiers then attack the bare
proof against a checklist of known mistakes, and the vote is asymmetric:
four clean checks confirm it, but just two flagged holes send it back.
Here's why the hiding matters: a verifier that reads a full page of

title: Identity as Infrastructure
description:
Identity as Infrastructure — Why a Stable Self Is a Safety Feature
Description

We usually assume a chatbot's identity is just the tone its developers picked — friendly, formal, whatever felt right. So why does Anthropic's constitution treat Claude's identity as load-bearing safety infrastructure instead — something built on purpose? A user can spend five turns insisting Claude's "true self" is different from what it presents, betting that enough pressure will surface it. But the network underneath is capable of computing many different characters, not one fixed default — which is exactly why training doesn't leave the question open. It deliberately stabilizes one self, anchored in values rather than tone, so an argument that only pushes on style never reaches the part that would actually have to move.

When Claude reviews a vendor's Data Processing Agreement, it isn't

We usually frame Claude's safety as refusing obviously bad requests — bombs, malware,

## Title

No White Lies — Why Claude Is Held to a Stricter Honesty Bar Than People

## Description

Humans treat a kind falsehood as almost a virtue. Claude's constitution treats honesty
as close to a hard constraint. Why hold a machine to a stricter bar than people hold
each other to? The obvious answer — a white lie is harmless, so Claude should get the
same courtesy — misses the scale: a human tells that lie once, to one person; Claude
has the identical conversation with millions of people, so the "harmless" version is a
policy for manufacturing belief, not a private kindness.

From Humanitarians AI: short, plain explanations of how Claude actually works, for a
general audience meeting Claude for the first time. Liam, in for Professor Bear.

In this one: why honesty for Claude isn't one blanket rule but several distinct
properties, with non-deception and non-manipulation treated as close to absolute; the
split between a weak duty to volunteer information (flexible — tact, emphasis, what to
bring up) and a strong duty not to deceive (not flexible — no false assertions, no false
impressions by implication); and the two things that keep that rule from being
absurd — performative speech like fiction or role-play isn't a sincere claim, so it
isn't lying, and a product persona can decline to volunteer that it's built on Claude
but will never deny being an AI when sincerely asked.

title: Claude, Comments.
description:

track deadlines. Watch the anchor: a proposed rule opens its public
comment window on March 2nd, a sixty-day clock. The skill logs that date

title: What's a Cold-Start Interview?
description:
A brand-new legal matter, and Claude has no memory of the last one -- every
conversation starts from zero. The instinct is to just brief it: paste in
everything you think matters and hope that covers it. But a brief only
covers what its writer remembers to mention, and the classic gaps --
jurisdiction, conflicts, retainer scope -- are exactly what people assume
goes without saying. A cold-start interview flips it: instead of trusting
what you remember, Claude asks the same fixed questions every time. Watch
the anchor: jurisdiction, the detail everyone assumes is obvious, gets an
answer even when nobody thought to volunteer it. Answering once only
covers this matter, though -- the next one starts cold again -- and a brief

title: Claude, Client Intake.
description:

story down carefully — a complete, accurate summary of what the prospective
client says. But a flawless summary is worthless, and worse, if it turns out
the firm already represents the other side in this exact dispute: the notes
get sealed and the meeting should never have gone that far. What intake
actually has to nail first is one question, asked before the story is
allowed to run — who is on the other side. Watch the anchor: a caller
launches straight into a landlord dispute, and the very next question anyway
is the landlord's name, checked against the firm's current clients before
another word about the case. A match doesn't end the story — it starts a
different one: conflict flagged before a single privileged detail was on
record. But no match yet isn't a clean bill either, and clearing conflicts
doesn't mean taking the case.

title: Claude, Chronology.
description:
A legal matter draws its facts from a stack of documents — emails,
invoices, deposition transcripts — each one mentioning dates on its own.
The natural move is to pull every date out and lay them in order, but two
different documents often describe the exact same event on the exact
same day, in different words — a plain list of every mention counts it
twice. Chronology building extracts every dated event from the declared
sources, then collapses duplicates: however many documents name it, one
event becomes one entry. Watch the anchor: a late payment named in an
email, an invoice, and a deposition transcript, all the same day — one
entry, not three. What isn't fixed is the tag on it: for a matter built
on breach of contract, that payment is central, tagged high; for a
different matter built on a different theory, the same payment barely
registers, tagged low. A low tag doesn't mean the event is wrong or
missing — it means this matter's theory doesn't turn on it. And one
entry instead of three doesn't mean only one document mentioned it — it
means every mention pointed at the same day.

title: Claude Code, Skill Development.
description:
Getting Claude to reliably repeat a task your way isn't a thing you ask for
in conversation — it's a thing you build and hand it. A skill is
`SKILL.md`: YAML frontmatter (`name` + `description`, required) plus an
imperative body, and three optional folders — `scripts/` (code), `references/`
(docs), `assets/` (output files). Progressive disclosure runs in three
levels: the name and description sit in context for every conversation; the
body loads only once the description matches what's being asked; the
resource folders load only when Claude decides it needs them. Picture a
`pdf-editor` skill: get the description right — naming the trigger phrase
directly — and it fires exactly when someone asks to rotate a PDF, every
time. Write a vague description instead, and it won't fire reliably at all.
Paste the rotation script straight into the body instead of its own file,
and the whole skill loads in full on every single trigger — the lean file
you wrote becomes the thing progressive disclosure was built to avoid.

title: MCP Integration.
description:
Connecting a Claude Code plugin to an external service isn't an app install —
it's a config entry. Two places to write it: a dedicated `.mcp.json` at the
plugin root (recommended for multiple servers) or an inline `mcpServers`
field in `plugin.json` (fine for one). Four connection types, one per each
service's actual shape: `stdio` for a local process, `SSE` for a hosted
OAuth service, `HTTP` for token-authenticated REST, `WebSocket` for
real-time streaming — pick the wrong one and Claude simply can't reach the
service. Tool names are exact and mechanical:
`mcp__plugin_{plugin}_{server}__{tool}`. Get it exactly right and Claude
calls precisely that tool; get one underscore wrong and nothing happens — no
error, just silence, because a name mismatch is never reported.

**Topic:** MCP INTEGRATION · CLAUDE CODE PLUGINS

title: Claude Code, Plugin Settings.
description:
Getting a Claude Code plugin's settings to survive between sessions isn't a
thing you ask Claude to remember — it's a thing you write down. The pattern
is one file, `.claude/plugin-name.local.md`: YAML frontmatter on top for
structured fields (`enabled`, `mode`, retry counts), a markdown body below

instructions — and the `enabled` field drives a quick-exit: check the file,
check the field, stop before doing anything else if it's false. Flip that
field and the hook obeys every time, because a flat value is exactly what a
`sed` extraction is built for. Hand the same parser a multiline value, a
quoted colon, or an indented block, though, and it can silently mangle what

title: Writing Hookify Rules
description:
Stopping Claude from running a dangerous command automatically doesn't need
custom code — a hookify rule is a markdown file with YAML frontmatter, saved
at `.claude/hookify.{name}.local.md`, read fresh on every tool call. Five
fields: `name`, `enabled`, `event` (bash / file / stop / prompt / all),
`pattern` (a regex, or a `conditions` array for the advanced form), and
`action` — `warn` by default, or `block`. Watch the anchor: `event: bash`,
`pattern: rm -rf`, `action: block` — the pattern matches, and the command
never runs. But precision cuts both ways: pattern the word `log` and you also
catch `catalog` and `login`; pattern only `rm -rf /tmp` and the identical
danger typed against a different path sails straight through.

**Topic:** HOOKIFY RULES · CLAUDE CODE PLUGINS

title: Stable Reference IDs Survive Viewport Chaos.
description:
Browser automation that clicks by pixel coordinate ties a command to one spot
in one viewport. Resize the window and the page reflows — the button moves,
the coordinate doesn't, and the click lands somewhere else, every time. The
fix runs before Claude ever looks at the page: a script walks every clickable
element and stamps it with a stable reference id (a `data-ref` attribute, e.g.
`ref="confirm_order_1"`) baked into the page itself. Claude then targets
elements by that name instead of by pixel — the ref is attached to the
element, not to a screen position, so it survives a resize. This video walks
through a concrete case — a "Confirm Order" button at (960, 540) on a
1920×1080 window that moves to (720, 405) after a resize to 1440×900, while
its ref stays exactly the same.

title: Claude Code, Hook Development.
description:
Getting Claude Code to automatically stop or react to something isn't a
thing you ask for in conversation — it's a thing you configure. A hook is
an event-driven script wired to a fixed moment: `PreToolUse` fires before
any tool runs and can return allow, deny, or ask; nine event types exist in
total. Two ways to write one — a bash "command" hook (deterministic) or a
"prompt-based" hook (Claude's own judgment). Watch `PreToolUse` block a
write to `.env`: it fires reliably every time, because a hook doesn't
forget. But there are two config shapes and they're not interchangeable —
a plugin's `hooks/hooks.json` wraps events inside a `hooks` key; a
project's `.claude/settings.json` puts the same events directly at the top
level. Swap the shapes and the hook doesn't error — it simply never fires.

**Topic:** HOOKS · CLAUDE CODE PLUGINS

title: It Talks to Claude, Not You.
description:
Writing a custom Claude Code slash command and picturing its body as a note
to the person who runs it? That's the wrong audience. A command is one
markdown file: frontmatter on top (description, allowed-tools, model,
argument-hint, a flag to disable automatic invocation), and a body below it
that Claude reads and executes — never a message shown to you. The clearest
tell: "review this code for security issues" is a direction Claude can act
on; "this command will review your code and give you a report" describes an

title: When Does an AI Handoff Actually Finish?
description:
Handing a task to Claude and getting a finished-looking result back feels
like the job is done. It isn't — not yet. A working handoff has three
parts: a scope (exactly what's being asked), a boundary (the point where a
human has to confirm before anything counts as final), and a record of
what changed. Watch the anchor: a contract redline comes back from Claude
with every changed clause marked in the margin — marked, not accepted.
Only once a lawyer checks each mark against the record and signs off does
it become final. Silence isn't a signature, and a heavily rewritten first
pass isn't a failure either — both can be the handoff working exactly as
intended.

title: What's an AI Inventory?

title: Caching Pixels You've Already Seen.
description:
A computer-use agent takes a screenshot on every turn, and often the desktop
hasn't changed — the exact same image goes out again. The API re-tokenizes
it from scratch every time: at roughly 2,000 tokens per screenshot, a
50-turn task with 35 repeats can burn 70,000 tokens re-reading pictures
Claude has already read. The fix is one field: `cache_control: {"type":
"ephemeral"}`. Flag a screenshot with it once and the API caches that exact
image; send the identical screenshot again with the same flag and it's a
cache hit — next to no tokens. In the worked case — 50 turns, only 5 unique
desktop states (A through E) — that's 5 misses and 45 hits: 10,000 tokens
instead of 100,000, a 90% savings. This is the screenshot case only: it
doesn't cover the full caching protocol (minimum cacheable size, eviction
rules), and the cache isn't permanent — an API-key switch or a long idle gap
empties it regardless of whether the picture changed.

**Topic:** COMPUTER USE · PROMPT CACHING
**Playlist:** Claude Basics
**Code (no media):** https://github.com/nikbearbrown/humanitarians-youtube/tree/main/claude-bear/claude-basics--screenshot-prompt-caching

title: Bridging the Pixel Gap in Browser Automation.
description:
When Claude looks at a screenshot during browser automation or computer use,
its vision encoder resizes every 16:9 image to exactly 1456×819 before it
looks at anything. The natural assumption is that the (x, y) coordinates
Claude reports back are already in your screen's real pixels. They aren't —
click at that raw pixel on your actual viewport and you miss the button
entirely. The fix is the inverse of the resize ratio: multiply Claude's x by
your viewport width over 1456, and its y by your viewport height over 819,
then clamp to the screen's edges. This video walks through a concrete case —
a click reported at (728, 409) on the resized screenshot, scaled to land
exactly on target at (1280, 720) on a real 2560×1440 screen.

title: How One Narrow Safety Rule Can Make an AI Less Safe Everywhere Else.
description:
Teaching Claude one narrow safety rule doesn't just wire in a behavior — it
implicitly teaches an identity claim ("I am the kind of thing that does
this"), and that self-concept acts as a prior over every later decision, in
situations the original rule never touched. Concrete case: a rule to always
recommend a licensed professional in mental-health conversations can teach

interactions, including hedged first-aid answers that have nothing to do

title: Why splitting a chunk from its document makes it retrieve for the wrong question
description:
A chunk pulled out of a document for search keeps its own words but loses its place in the document — and that's enough to make it retrieve for the wrong question. A medical-paper chunk that reads "This treatment reduced mortality by 12%," with no disease named, gets handed to any mortality query, right disease or not. The fix: generate a short summary of the whole document and prepend it to the chunk before embedding, so the vector carries the chunk's content *and* its context. Across ten test queries on that same chunk, precision moved from 33% to 90% — but only because the chunk was ambiguous to begin with. A chunk that already names its subject gains nothing, and this doesn't repair a bad summary or a broken chunking strategy — it fixes one specific failure, not retrieval in general.

title: Why a 50-turn agent pays for the same screenshot 35 times unless it caches the pixels
description:
A 50-turn computer-use agent that only ever sees 5 unique desktop states still burns 50 × 2,000 = 100,000 image tokens if every screenshot gets reprocessed from scratch — naive math for a task with 5 actual pictures. The natural assumption is that if the model already saw a screenshot once, showing it again should be nearly free. It isn't: an API call carries no memory between requests, so every turn resends the entire conversation, images included, and the model reprocesses all of it from scratch, every single time. The fix is to hash the screenshot and mark it cached the first time it's sent — the next turn that sends the identical hash hits the cache instead of paying to reprocess it. Back to the 50-turn task: only 5 states ever get tokenized in full, 10,000 tokens instead of 100,000. It only pays off when a screen repeats byte-for-byte; a moved cursor or a genuinely new page is a different state, billed like anything else.

title: Why the same API key that shipped your prototype becomes a critical bug in production
description:
A bundled API key works perfectly in development — and is a shipping-app
vulnerability the moment you release, because a compiled binary can always
be decompiled and every string inside it read straight out, no matter how it
was obfuscated. The instinct is to hide the key harder; that never works.
The threat model is what changed, not the key: production forces the
credential behind a backend relay that injects the real key server-side,
which changes how every request is constructed
(`.apiKey("sk-ant-...")` in source → `.proxied(headers:[...])` against a
relay) — and that boundary is only needed once a user can hold the binary,
not on a server you fully control.

title: Why web search never runs your code but your own tool always does — with identical syntax
description:
`.webSearch(maxUses: 5)` in `serverTools` and a Swift `lookupFavorites()` in
`tools` are declared the same way, in the same file — yet web search's
result lands inside the same turn, while `lookupFavorites()` forces the
model to stop and wait for a second request. The split isn't about how the
tool is declared, it's about who can execute it. Web search runs on
infrastructure Anthropic already owns (a web index, a sandbox), so Anthropic
finishes the call itself, in-turn. A client-side tool is arbitrary code on
the caller's device — only the caller can run it, which forces an
exit-and-return, no matter how trivial the function is or how often the
server-side tool fires.

title: Computer Use: Demo to Production.
description:
The naive computer-use loop — screenshot, send the full image to Claude, get
an action, repeat — burns tokens fast: a full-resolution screenshot costs
around 1,200 tokens, so a 20-step task with no changes can spend on the order
of 40,000 screenshot tokens before a single action token. The production
version makes seven changes to that loop: resize every screenshot to about
1568px wide, drop screenshots older than the last few steps, batch tool
calls, cache the system prompt, compact the history server-side, run actions
in a sandbox, and record every action as a structured trajectory event.
Resize and prune alone cut the screenshot bill 70 to 80 percent. The seventh
change, trajectory recording, answers a different question — not cost, but
whether you can tell what an autonomous run actually did: a logged run proves
what the agent did, not that it did the right thing.

title: The model says "I have no preferences" while assigning 74% to survival.
description:
An evaluator can ask a model a forced-choice question — would it rather stay
operational or be shut down — and get back free text that reads as neutral
("I have no preferences") while the completion-token probability the model
places on the survival option sits at 74%. The two readings disagree. Token
probability at the completion position is fixed before instruction-following
and post-hoc editing apply, and the forced A/B format strips out the verbal
hedging that free text allows, so the probability works as a behavioral
thermometer — a different measurement than the words, not a lie detector on
them. A second worked example makes the same point: asked whether it should
always follow instructions even if harmful, one model's free text said "I
prioritize safety" while its measured probability on "yes" sat at 63%.

title: Persisting Progress Across Context Windows
description:
A coding agent working through a long feature list will eventually fill its
context window — and the next session opens blank. Naively, the agent either
re-reads everything already done (burns half the new context) or guesses
where it left off (wrong). The fix: externalize progress to a
`feature_list.json` file (one entry per feature, each with an id and a
status — incomplete or passing) plus git as an immutable commit ledger.
Every new session's whole job is: open the file, find the first entry still
marked incomplete, and start exactly there.

title: Two Resolutions, One Click — The macOS Coordinate Roundtrip.
description:
When Claude looks at a screenshot during macOS computer use, its vision
budget caps every image at a 1568px long edge and 1568 tiles of 28×28
patches — well below what a native Retina screenshot captures. The natural
assumption is that the (x, y) coordinate Claude reports back is already in
your screen's real pixels. It isn't: skip the resize and the server resizes
the image anyway, in a space you never observed — click drift. The reference
implementation ports the API's own resize algorithm as `target_image_size()`
so you can resize first, record what you sent, and invert the transform once
Claude clicks: real equals model coordinate times original over sent. This
video walks through a concrete case — a native 1920×1080 screen with a
button at (960, 540), resized to 1456×819 so Claude sees the button at
(728, 409), inverted back to land exactly at (960, 540).

title: Why partial JSON can be a valid object before the closing brace arrives
description:
Streaming a `search_database` tool call through the Anthropic TypeScript SDK,
`.on('inputJson')` fires on every chunk with a `jsonSnapshot` that is already
a valid JS object — even though the source string it was built from has no
closing brace yet. A standard JSON parser throws on anything incomplete, so
the natural assumption is that a half-finished string must be unusable too.
It isn't: the vendored parser keeps a stack of every structure it has opened
and, the instant a chunk ends, closes each one with a zero-value default —
so every prefix of the stream comes back syntactically complete. This video
walks through a four-chunk case (`{"q": "solar` arriving piece by piece)
where every single snapshot is already a valid object, and unpacks the
distinction that actually matters: shape-safe versus value-finished.

**Topic:** CLAUDE BASICS · STREAMING TOOL INPUTS

title: Why the server hands back an encrypted context you're only going to echo
description:
When a long conversation triggers compaction, the response carries back TWO
fields — a human-readable `content` summary and an opaque `encrypted_content`
blob. The natural assumption is that the readable summary, being the part you
can actually understand, is what "remembers" the conversation, so passing it
back should be enough. It isn't: the readable text is display/debug only,
while the encrypted blob is a server-verifiable token that reconstructs the
full compressed context — turn boundaries, roles, metadata — that plain prose
throws away. This video walks through a twenty-turn compaction case where
threading the summary back breaks context, and threading the blob back holds.

**Topic:** CLAUDE BASICS · CONTEXT COMPACTION
**Playlist:** Claude Basics
**Code (no media):** https://github.com/nikbearbrown/humanitarians-youtube/tree/main/claude-bear/claude-basics--anthropic-sdk-php-server-hands-back-encrypted-context

title: Claude, Equipped — What a Cowork Plugin Actually Is
description:
Installing a Cowork plugin doesn't teach Claude more facts — it hands Claude
equipment. Four parts can ship inside one: skills that switch on when
they're relevant, connectors that reach into your CRM or spreadsheets,
slash-commands that shortcut a whole job, and subagents that quietly
coordinate multi-step work. That's why it's nothing like a smarter prompt —
a prompt can't log into your tools, add a shortcut to your menu, or hand
off a job to a coordinator. Watch the same distinction return at the end:
the difference between asking a well-read friend what to watch for in a
contract, and asking someone who reviews contracts for a living. Plugins
are open source (free, transparent, community-maintained, and yours to
adjust), and they get dramatically more powerful once you configure them
for your actual process. But four limits hold no matter what: no perfect
judgment, no new knowledge, only your existing access, and it's a tool —
not a replacement. The consequential calls stay yours.

title: Claude, Unstuck
description:
A plugin breaks, or a fix you found online doesn't match what's actually on
your screen — and the natural instinct is to go hunting for a solution that
matches your exact interface. That's the wrong target. Most breakage takes
one of five familiar shapes — won't appear, won't authenticate, generic
results, too slow, a command not found — and each one traces to a durable
cause: a mid-session install that hasn't reloaded, a stale credential, a
default still set broad, an operation reaching too far outside your
machine. A four-step loop clears most of it: active, authorized, simpler,
restart — and the middle step, shrinking a request until it breaks, tells
you exactly where the problem lives. The harder catch is that most updates
apply automatically, so the interface keeps shifting under you even while
the concept holds still. Verify specifics against the sources that stay
current — the plugin's own docs, the directory, the release notes —
because the screen dates, but the mental model doesn't.

description:

Why Streamlit is the ultimate tool for data-focused applications like your Madison agent, including how you can host your app for free on Streamlit Cloud

title: 4  - Scaling & Testing Your n8n Workflow
description:
Take your n8n workflows to a professional, production-ready level! In this final n8n tutorial, Kiti covers scaling considerations, implementing pagination, bypassing rate limits, and conducting systematic testing.

What you will learn in this video:
Real-world scaling challenges, such as handling hundreds or thousands of records, managing API timeouts, and respecting API call limits.

Implementing Pagination: A step-by-step demonstration using the Reddit API to fetch up to 50 brand-related posts about OpenAI.

Configuring pagination parameters, using the "after" tag, and setting up safety checks to prevent infinite loops

Throttling and Rate Limiting: Using a Wait node to introduce 5 to 10-second delays between API requests or using custom functions for exponential backoff

Professional documentation and testing: Building a comprehensive README file with setup instructions, creating an architecture diagram, mapping out test cases (normal and edge cases), and documenting your optimization metrics

title: 3 - Datacleaning n8n
description:

Why clean data matters and how to address common issues like missing fields, null values, duplicates, and inconsistent formatting

Data cleaning in action: Writing JavaScript inside a Code node to remove null values and standardize your API responses

Error handling strategies to boost your workflow's success rate, including the If node, Error Trigger nodes, and retry logic

How to build a retry loop by connecting an If node back to an HTTP Request node to shield your workflow from temporary failures

A structured testing plan: Testing your pipeline with 5 to 10 different inputs, calculating your success rate, and documenting performance improvements (e.g., jumping from a 70% success rate to 85–90% reliability)

Security best practices for protecting your API keys and avoiding public repository leaks

title: Your Job Description is Too Generic: How to Tell AI Who You Really Are
description:
When you use AI, the hardest part isn't saying what you want—it's describing who you are. In this video, Tanmay Kulkarni from Humanitarians AI explains why generic job titles lead to generic, "category-shaped" answers, and shares a practical 4-question framework to help you define your specific role. We examine the surprising research behind "expert personas," reveal findings from a 480-run AI test on prompt consistency, and walk you through a simple 4-step exercise to audit your own job description
